units.title: Matter waves-wave nature of particles, de-Broglie relation.
Dual nature of radiation, Photoelectric effect, Hertz and Lenard's observations;

questions.unit: Matter waves-wave nature of particles, de-Broglie relation.
questions.stem: What is the de Broglie wavelength of a ball of mass 0.10 kg moving at $10\,\text{m s}^{-1}$? (Take $h = 6.63\times10^{-34}\,\text{J s}$.)

questions.unit: Matter waves-wave nature of particles, de-Broglie relation.
questions.stem: A particle has momentum 6.63 × 10⁻²⁴ kg m s⁻¹. What is its de Broglie wavelength? (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)

questions.unit: Matter waves-wave nature of particles, de-Broglie relation.
questions.stem: Which of the following correctly states de Broglie's hypothesis of matter waves?

options.label: A
options.text: Only charged particles moving in electric fields behave like waves

options.label: B
options.text: Every moving material particle has a wave associated with it, of wavelength λ = h/p

options.label: C
options.text: Electrons in atoms emit matter waves whenever they jump between orbits

options.label: D
options.text: Light consists of particles called photons, each of energy hν

questions.unit: Matter waves-wave nature of particles, de-Broglie relation.
questions.stem:
Assertion (A): An electron microscope can resolve much finer detail than an optical microscope.
Reason (R): Fast electrons have a de Broglie wavelength much smaller than that of visible light.

options.label: A
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.unit: Matter waves-wave nature of particles, de-Broglie relation.
questions.stem: Panel (b) of the figure shows the de Broglie wavelength λ plotted against 1/p, where p is the momentum of the particle. The graph is a straight line through the origin. What does its slope represent?

questions.unit: Matter waves-wave nature of particles, de-Broglie relation.
questions.stem: If the momentum of a particle is doubled, its de Broglie wavelength is:

questions.unit: Matter waves-wave nature of particles, de-Broglie relation.
questions.stem: Why is the wave nature of a moving cricket ball never observed?

options.label: A
options.text: A cricket ball has no matter wave because it carries no charge

options.label: B
options.text: Its de Broglie wavelength is too large to be measured

options.label: C
options.text: Matter waves exist only for particles moving close to the speed of light

options.label: D
options.text: Its de Broglie wavelength (of the order of 10⁻³⁴ m) is far smaller than any slit or obstacle, so diffraction cannot be detected

questions.unit: Matter waves-wave nature of particles, de-Broglie relation.
questions.stem: De Broglie explained Bohr's quantisation rule by requiring a whole number of wavelengths to fit around the orbit, $2\pi r = n\lambda$. The radius of the n-th Bohr orbit of hydrogen is $r_n = n^2 a_0$ with $a_0 = 0.529\times10^{-10}\,\text{m}$. What is the de Broglie wavelength of the electron in the n = 3 orbit?

questions.unit: Matter waves-wave nature of particles, de-Broglie relation.
questions.stem: A photon and an electron each have a wavelength of 1.0 nm. What is the ratio of the energy of the photon to the kinetic energy of the electron? (Take $h = 6.63\times10^{-34}\,\text{J s}$, $c = 3.0\times10^{8}\,\text{m s}^{-1}$ and $m_e = 9.1\times10^{-31}\,\text{kg}$.)

questions.unit: Matter waves-wave nature of particles, de-Broglie relation.
questions.stem: A proton and an alpha particle, each starting from rest, are accelerated through the same potential difference V. Taking the mass of the alpha particle as 4mₚ and its charge as 2e, what is the ratio λₚ/λ_α of their de Broglie wavelengths?

questions.unit: Matter waves-wave nature of particles, de-Broglie relation.
questions.stem:
Read the following statements:
A. Diffraction of electrons by crystals, observed by Davisson and Germer and by G. P. Thomson in 1927, confirmed de Broglie's hypothesis.
B. The square of the amplitude of a particle's matter wave at a point is proportional to the probability of finding the particle there.
C. An electron accelerated from rest through 54 V has a de Broglie wavelength of about 0.167 nm.
D. The matter waves of all particles travel at the speed of light in vacuum.
Which of the statements given above are correct?

questions.unit: Matter waves-wave nature of particles, de-Broglie relation.
questions.stem:
Assertion (A): A photon and an electron (v ≪ c) that have the same de Broglie wavelength do not have the same energy; the photon has much more energy.
Reason (R): A photon has a greater momentum than an electron of the same de Broglie wavelength.

options.label: A
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.unit: Matter waves-wave nature of particles, de-Broglie relation.
questions.stem: Electrons starting from rest are accelerated through the potential differences in List-I. Match each with the approximate de Broglie wavelength in List-II.

questions.unit: Matter waves-wave nature of particles, de-Broglie relation.
questions.stem: The kinetic energy of a free electron is increased by 44%. By what percentage does its de Broglie wavelength change?

questions.unit: Matter waves-wave nature of particles, de-Broglie relation.
questions.stem: An electron has a de Broglie wavelength of 1.0 nm. What is its kinetic energy? (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, mₑ = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg, 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J)

questions.unit: Matter waves-wave nature of particles, de-Broglie relation.
questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about matter waves:
A. Matter waves are electromagnetic waves emitted by moving particles.
B. The de Broglie wavelength of a particle depends on its momentum and not on its charge.
C. For the same kinetic energy, a lighter particle has a longer de Broglie wavelength.
D. The de Broglie wavelength of a particle increases when its speed increases.
Which of the statements given above are correct?

questions.unit: Matter waves-wave nature of particles, de-Broglie relation.
questions.stem: Match each situation in List-I with the expression for the associated wavelength in List-II (k_B is Boltzmann's constant).

left: B. Particle of mass m with kinetic energy K
C. Particle of mass m and charge q accelerated from rest through potential difference V
D. Gas molecule of mass m in thermal equilibrium at temperature T

questions.unit: Matter waves-wave nature of particles, de-Broglie relation.
questions.stem: A neutron in thermal equilibrium at 300 K has an average kinetic energy of $\tfrac32 k_BT$. What is its de Broglie wavelength? Use $k_B = 1.38\times10^{-23}\,\text{J K}^{-1}$, $m_n = 1.67\times10^{-27}\,\text{kg}$ and $h = 6.63\times10^{-34}\,\text{J s}$.

questions.unit: Matter waves-wave nature of particles, de-Broglie relation.
questions.stem: A neutron has a de Broglie wavelength of 0.10 nm. What is its kinetic energy in electron volt? (Take $h = 6.63\times10^{-34}\,\text{J s}$, $m_n = 1.67\times10^{-27}\,\text{kg}$ and $e = 1.6\times10^{-19}\,\text{C}$.)

questions.unit: Matter waves-wave nature of particles, de-Broglie relation.
questions.stem: What is the de Broglie wavelength of an electron moving with a speed of 1.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹? (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, mₑ = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg)

questions.unit: Matter waves-wave nature of particles, de-Broglie relation.
questions.stem:
Assertion (A): A neutron, being electrically neutral, has no de Broglie wave associated with it.
Reason (R): The de Broglie wavelength of a particle depends only on its momentum, λ = h/p.

options.label: A
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.unit: Matter waves-wave nature of particles, de-Broglie relation.
questions.stem:
Assertion (A): Electrons accelerated through about 50–100 V are diffracted by a crystal, much as X-rays are.
Reason (R): Electrons are negatively charged particles.

options.label: A
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.unit: Matter waves-wave nature of particles, de-Broglie relation.
questions.stem: In the electron gun shown, electrons leave the cathode practically at rest and emerge through the anode with a de Broglie wavelength of 0.0388 nm. What is the accelerating potential difference V?

questions.unit: Matter waves-wave nature of particles, de-Broglie relation.
questions.stem: An electron starting from rest is accelerated through a potential difference of 400 V. What is its de Broglie wavelength approximately?

questions.unit: Matter waves-wave nature of particles, de-Broglie relation.
questions.stem: In the Davisson-Germer experiment, electrons were accelerated through 54 V. What is the de Broglie wavelength of such electrons? (Take $h = 6.63\times10^{-34}\,\text{J s}$, $m_e = 9.1\times10^{-31}\,\text{kg}$ and $e = 1.6\times10^{-19}\,\text{C}$.)

questions.unit: Matter waves-wave nature of particles, de-Broglie relation.
questions.stem:
Assertion (A): The de Broglie wavelength of an electron decreases when the potential difference through which it is accelerated is increased.
Reason (R): For an electron accelerated from rest through a potential difference V, λ = h/√(2meV).

options.label: A
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.unit: Matter waves-wave nature of particles, de-Broglie relation.
questions.stem: The graph shows the de Broglie wavelength of an electron against the accelerating potential. At 100 V the wavelength is about 0.123 nm. What accelerating potential would make the wavelength about 0.0307 nm, one-quarter of this value?

questions.unit: Matter waves-wave nature of particles, de-Broglie relation.
questions.stem: An electron and a proton are moving with the same speed. What is the ratio of the de Broglie wavelength of the electron to that of the proton? (mₑ = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg, mₚ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg)

questions.unit: Matter waves-wave nature of particles, de-Broglie relation.
questions.stem: An electron and a proton, each starting from rest, are accelerated through the same potential difference. What is the ratio λₑ/λₚ of their de Broglie wavelengths? (mₚ/mₑ ≈ 1835)

questions.unit: Matter waves-wave nature of particles, de-Broglie relation.
questions.stem: An electron and a proton have equal de Broglie wavelengths. Which of them has the greater kinetic energy?

options.label: A
options.text: The proton, because it is heavier

options.label: B
options.text: Both have equal kinetic energy because they have equal momentum

options.label: C
options.text: The electron, because K = p²/2m and its mass is much smaller

options.label: D
options.text: It cannot be decided without knowing their speeds

questions.unit: Dual nature of radiation, Photoelectric effect, Hertz and Lenard's observations;
questions.stem: The work function of a metal is 2.48 eV. What is its threshold wavelength? (Take hc = 1240 eV nm.)

questions.unit: Dual nature of radiation, Photoelectric effect, Hertz and Lenard's observations;
questions.stem: Panel (a) of the figure shows that photocurrent is a straight line through the origin when plotted against intensity, and panel (b) shows a horizontal line for stopping potential against intensity. Together these graphs show that:

options.label: A
options.text: intensity changes the number of photoelectrons emitted per second but not their maximum kinetic energy

options.label: B
options.text: intensity changes the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons but not their number

options.label: C
options.text: intensity changes neither the number nor the energy of the photoelectrons

options.label: D
options.text: a minimum intensity is needed before any photoelectrons are emitted

questions.unit: Dual nature of radiation, Photoelectric effect, Hertz and Lenard's observations;
questions.stem: Ultraviolet light of wavelength 310 nm falls on a metal surface of work function 2.5 eV. What is the stopping potential? (hc = 1240 eV nm)

questions.unit: Dual nature of radiation, Photoelectric effect, Hertz and Lenard's observations;
questions.stem: Very dim ultraviolet light of frequency above the threshold is switched on and falls on a zinc plate. When does photoelectric emission begin?

options.label: A
options.text: Only after the light has been on long enough for the electrons to store energy, possibly hours

options.label: B
options.text: Only if the intensity exceeds a certain threshold intensity

options.label: D
options.text: After a delay that is inversely proportional to the frequency

questions.unit: Dual nature of radiation, Photoelectric effect, Hertz and Lenard's observations;
questions.stem: What is the momentum of a photon of wavelength 663 nm? (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)

questions.unit: Dual nature of radiation, Photoelectric effect, Hertz and Lenard's observations;
questions.stem: The frequency of light falling on a photosensitive surface is increased (staying above threshold) while the number of photons striking it per second is kept the same. What happens?

options.label: A
options.text: The maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons increases and the saturation current stays the same

options.label: B
options.text: The maximum kinetic energy stays the same and the saturation current increases

options.label: C
options.text: Both the maximum kinetic energy and the saturation current increase

options.label: D
options.text: Both the maximum kinetic energy and the saturation current decrease

questions.unit: Dual nature of radiation, Photoelectric effect, Hertz and Lenard's observations;
questions.stem: In his 1887 experiments with spark gaps, Hertz found that sparks across the detector gap jumped more readily when the emitter plate was illuminated by:

options.label: B
options.text: ultraviolet light from an arc lamp

options.label: C
options.text: infrared radiation from a hot body

options.label: D
options.text: radio waves produced by the transmitter itself

questions.unit: Dual nature of radiation, Photoelectric effect, Hertz and Lenard's observations;
questions.stem: Which one of the following phenomena can be explained only by treating light as a stream of particles (photons) and not by the wave theory?

questions.unit: Dual nature of radiation, Photoelectric effect, Hertz and Lenard's observations;
questions.stem: In a graph of stopping potential V₀ (y-axis) against frequency ν of incident light (x-axis) for a photosensitive metal, the slope of the straight line is equal to:

questions.unit: Dual nature of radiation, Photoelectric effect, Hertz and Lenard's observations;
questions.stem: The work function of a metal is best described as:

options.label: A
options.text: the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons emitted from the metal

options.label: B
options.text: the energy of the incident photon at which the photocurrent reaches saturation

options.label: C
options.text: the minimum energy that must be supplied to an electron to just remove it from the metal surface

options.label: D
options.text: the energy needed to remove the most tightly bound electron from an atom of the metal

questions.unit: Dual nature of radiation, Photoelectric effect, Hertz and Lenard's observations;
questions.stem: Light of wavelength 500 nm and power 4.0 mW falls on the cathode of a photocell. Only 0.5% of the incident photons eject electrons. What is the saturation photocurrent? (hc = 1.989 × 10⁻²⁵ J m, e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)

questions.unit: Dual nature of radiation, Photoelectric effect, Hertz and Lenard's observations;
questions.stem: In a photoelectric experiment, the stopping potential is 0.60 V for light of frequency 6.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz and 1.85 V for light of frequency 9.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz. What is the threshold frequency of the metal?

questions.unit: Dual nature of radiation, Photoelectric effect, Hertz and Lenard's observations;
questions.stem: When light of wavelength 400 nm falls on a metal surface, the stopping potential is 0.80 V. What will the stopping potential be when light of wavelength 300 nm falls on the same surface? (hc = 1240 eV nm)

questions.unit: Dual nature of radiation, Photoelectric effect, Hertz and Lenard's observations;
questions.stem: A metal has threshold frequency ν₀. It is illuminated first with light of frequency 2ν₀ and then with light of frequency 5ν₀. What is the ratio of the maximum speeds of the photoelectrons in the two cases?

questions.unit: Dual nature of radiation, Photoelectric effect, Hertz and Lenard's observations;
questions.stem: When a metal is illuminated with light of wavelength λ, the stopping potential is 3V₀. When it is illuminated with light of wavelength 2λ, the stopping potential is V₀. What is the threshold wavelength of the metal?

questions.unit: Dual nature of radiation, Photoelectric effect, Hertz and Lenard's observations;
questions.stem: A metal surface is illuminated first with light of wavelength 250 nm and then with light of wavelength 350 nm. The work function of the metal is not given, but both wavelengths cause emission. What is the difference between the two stopping potentials? (hc = 1240 eV nm)

options.label: C
options.text: It cannot be found without the work function

questions.unit: Dual nature of radiation, Photoelectric effect, Hertz and Lenard's observations;
questions.stem: Light of wavelength 250 nm falls on a metal whose work function is 2.0 eV. What is the maximum speed of the emitted photoelectrons? (hc = 1240 eV nm, mₑ = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg, e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)

questions.unit: Dual nature of radiation, Photoelectric effect, Hertz and Lenard's observations;
questions.stem: Light of frequency above threshold falls on a metal in a photocell. Match each change in List-I with its effect in List-II.

left: B. Frequency increased, photon flux unchanged
C. Metal replaced by one with a larger work function (frequency still above its threshold)
D. Frequency reduced below the threshold frequency
right: I. Stopping potential decreases but stays non-zero
II. Photocurrent becomes zero for every intensity
III. Saturation current doubles, stopping potential unchanged
IV. Stopping potential increases, saturation current unchanged

questions.unit: Dual nature of radiation, Photoelectric effect, Hertz and Lenard's observations;
questions.stem:
Assertion (A): Light whose frequency is below the threshold frequency of a metal can eject photoelectrons from it if the light is made sufficiently intense.
Reason (R): The threshold frequency ν₀ of a metal is related to its work function φ₀ by φ₀ = hν₀.

options.label: A
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.unit: Dual nature of radiation, Photoelectric effect, Hertz and Lenard's observations;
questions.stem: Monochromatic light falls on a metal, yet the photoelectrons come out with a range of kinetic energies from zero up to a maximum value K_max. Why do they not all have the same kinetic energy?

options.label: A
options.text: Electrons come from different depths and energy levels, and those from inside lose energy before escaping; only the least bound surface electrons leave with K_max

options.label: B
options.text: Different photons in monochromatic light have different energies

options.label: C
options.text: Each electron absorbs a different number of photons

options.label: D
options.text: The work function differs from electron to electron because of their different charges

questions.unit: Dual nature of radiation, Photoelectric effect, Hertz and Lenard's observations;
questions.stem: A V₀–ν graph is drawn for a metal. The metal is then replaced by another metal of larger work function and the graph is drawn again. How does the new line compare with the first?

options.label: A
options.text: It has a larger slope and passes through the same threshold frequency

options.label: B
options.text: It has a smaller slope and a larger threshold frequency

options.label: C
options.text: It is parallel to the first line and shifted to the right, with a larger threshold frequency

options.label: D
options.text: It is parallel to the first line and shifted to the left, with a smaller threshold frequency

questions.unit: Dual nature of radiation, Photoelectric effect, Hertz and Lenard's observations;
questions.stem: The figure shows stopping potential against frequency for two metals. Light of frequency 10 × 10¹⁴ Hz falls on each metal in turn. Using the graph (h/e ≈ 4.14 × 10⁻¹⁵ V s), which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Both metals emit electrons, and those from metal 2 have the larger maximum kinetic energy

options.label: B
options.text: Metal 1 emits electrons with a maximum kinetic energy of about 2.0 eV, while metal 2 emits no electrons

options.label: C
options.text: Metal 1 emits electrons with a maximum kinetic energy of about 4.1 eV, and metal 2 with about 2.0 eV

options.label: D
options.text: Neither metal emits electrons at this frequency

questions.unit: Dual nature of radiation, Photoelectric effect, Hertz and Lenard's observations;
questions.stem: The figure shows photocurrent against collector plate potential for light of one frequency at three intensities I₁ < I₂ < I₃. All three curves reach zero current at the same potential −V₀. What does this common cut-off point tell us?

options.label: A
options.text: The work function of the metal increases with intensity

options.label: B
options.text: The number of photoelectrons emitted per second is independent of intensity

options.label: C
options.text: The saturation current is independent of intensity

options.label: D
options.text: The maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons is independent of intensity

questions.unit: Dual nature of radiation, Photoelectric effect, Hertz and Lenard's observations;
questions.stem:
Assertion (A): For a given metal and light of a fixed frequency above threshold, doubling the intensity of the light does not change the stopping potential.
Reason (R): The maximum kinetic energy of a photoelectron is decided by the energy of a single photon, and the energy of each photon depends only on the frequency.

options.label: A
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.unit: Dual nature of radiation, Photoelectric effect, Hertz and Lenard's observations;
questions.stem: In the photoelectric experiment, a photocurrent flows even when the potential of the collector plate relative to the emitter is zero. The reason is that:

options.label: A
options.text: the light itself carries charge to the collector

options.label: B
options.text: the collector is also illuminated and emits electrons towards the emitter

options.label: C
options.text: the emitter acquires a positive charge which pushes electrons to the collector

options.label: D
options.text: the photoelectrons leave the emitter with kinetic energy, so many of them reach the collector without any accelerating field

questions.unit: Dual nature of radiation, Photoelectric effect, Hertz and Lenard's observations;
questions.stem:
Assertion (A): The graphs of stopping potential against frequency for two different metals are parallel straight lines.
Reason (R): For light of a given frequency above threshold, the photoelectric current is directly proportional to the intensity of the light.

options.label: A
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.unit: Dual nature of radiation, Photoelectric effect, Hertz and Lenard's observations;
questions.stem:
Read the following statements about photons:
A. The energy of a photon depends on the frequency of the radiation and not on its intensity.
B. Photons are deflected by electric and magnetic fields because they carry energy.
C. In a collision between a photon and an electron, the total energy and the total momentum are conserved.
D. The total number of photons is conserved in every interaction of radiation with matter.
Which of the statements given above are correct?

questions.stem: The threshold frequency of a metal is 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Light of frequency 8.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz falls on it. What is the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted photoelectrons? (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J)

questions.unit: Dual nature of radiation, Photoelectric effect, Hertz and Lenard's observations;
questions.stem: In a photoelectric experiment the intensity of the incident light is doubled while its frequency (above threshold) is kept the same. Which of the following is the correct result?

options.label: B
options.text: The maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons doubles

options.label: C
options.text: The threshold frequency of the metal is halved

options.label: D
options.text: The saturation current doubles and the stopping potential is unchanged

questions.unit: Dual nature of radiation, Photoelectric effect, Hertz and Lenard's observations;
questions.stem: The figure shows photocurrent against collector plate potential for light of three frequencies ν₁, ν₂ and ν₃ falling on the same metal with the same photon flux. Which conclusion follows from the figure?

options.label: A
options.text: The photoelectrons produced by ν₁ have the greatest maximum kinetic energy

options.label: B
options.text: The saturation current is greatest for ν₃

options.label: C
options.text: Since V₀₃ is the largest stopping potential, ν₃ is the highest frequency and gives the most energetic photoelectrons

options.label: D
options.text: The work function of the metal is different for each of the three frequencies

questions.unit: Dual nature of radiation, Photoelectric effect, Hertz and Lenard's observations;

left: A. Work function of the metal

questions.unit: Dual nature of radiation, Photoelectric effect, Hertz and Lenard's observations;
questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about the early experiments of Hallwachs and Lenard on photoelectric emission:
A. A negatively charged zinc plate connected to an electroscope loses its charge when ultraviolet light falls on it.
B. An uncharged zinc plate becomes negatively charged when ultraviolet light falls on it.
C. In an evacuated tube, a current flowed between the emitter and the collector when ultraviolet light fell on the emitter, and it stopped when the light was cut off.
D. Zinc did not emit electrons when illuminated by visible light, however intense the light was.
Which of the statements given above are correct?

questions.unit: Dual nature of radiation, Photoelectric effect, Hertz and Lenard's observations;
questions.stem:
Assertion (A): The saturation photocurrent increases when the intensity of light of a fixed frequency (above threshold) is increased.
Reason (R): Increasing the intensity of light increases the energy of each photon.

options.label: A
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.unit: Dual nature of radiation, Photoelectric effect, Hertz and Lenard's observations;
questions.stem: What is the energy, in electron volts, of a photon of frequency 1.5 × 10¹⁵ Hz? (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J)

questions.unit: Dual nature of radiation, Photoelectric effect, Hertz and Lenard's observations;
questions.stem: Match each scientist in List-I with their contribution to the photoelectric effect in List-II.

right: I. Careful measurements of stopping potential against frequency that confirmed the photoelectric equation and gave a value of h
II. Proposed that radiation consists of quanta of energy hν, each absorbed whole by one electron
III. Noticed that sparks across a detector gap jumped more easily under ultraviolet illumination
IV. Showed with an evacuated two-electrode tube that ultraviolet light on the emitter drives a current carried by electrons

questions.unit: Dual nature of radiation, Photoelectric effect, Hertz and Lenard's observations;
questions.stem: The work functions of five metals are: caesium 2.14 eV, potassium 2.30 eV, sodium 2.75 eV, calcium 3.20 eV and copper 4.65 eV. Light of wavelength 500 nm falls on each. Which metals emit photoelectrons? (hc = 1240 eV nm)

questions.unit: Dual nature of radiation, Photoelectric effect, Hertz and Lenard's observations;
questions.stem: In the apparatus shown, the commutator is used to make the collector A negative with respect to the emitter C, and this negative potential is slowly increased in magnitude. Frequency and intensity of the light are kept constant. How does the reading of the microammeter change?

options.label: A
options.text: It increases steadily until it reaches the saturation value

options.label: B
options.text: It stays constant, because the number of photoelectrons emitted is unchanged

options.label: C
options.text: It reverses direction once A becomes negative

options.label: D
options.text: It decreases and becomes zero at a definite potential that does not depend on the intensity of light

questions.unit: Dual nature of radiation, Photoelectric effect, Hertz and Lenard's observations;
questions.stem:
The classical wave theory of light makes several predictions about photoelectric emission. Consider:
A. The maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons should increase with the intensity of light.
B. There should be a threshold frequency below which no electrons are emitted.
